title: LIPAR: Latent Inter-Frame Pruning with Attention Recovery
claim: Our efficiency method preserves output quality across editing tasks while being faster, lighter on memory, and preferred over the baseline.
layout: Left and right sample grids, top-to-bottom frames, bottom metric bars
description: The figure has two sample galleries side by side. On the left, a column of input video frames, with the face blurred, sits next to three stylized outputs: Robot, Cartoon Santa and King. Each column shows three frames, separated by vertical ellipses, and the head turns from frame to frame. Gray masked regions in the input frames mark the temporally unchanged latents that get reused. On the right, a warped input video sits next to a TTM output showing a red liquid being poured into a glass. Yellow headers label the output columns. A strip of bars along the bottom compares LIPAR with Self-Forcing. LIPAR gets 12.2 FPS against 8.4 FPS (45% faster) and 18.56 GB against 26.24 GB (29% smaller), plus a win/draw/loss preference bar of 18.4%, 68.3% and 13.3%. Green marks ours and tan marks the baseline. The eye goes first to the large photo grid.
caption: We present LIPAR, a pruning framework that increases inference speed and reduces GPU memory usage for conditioned video generation by reusing temporally unchanged latents (gray regions). With our proposed Attention Recovery, LIPAR integrates with the Diffusion Transformer seamlessly in a training-free manner without degrading visual quality.
abstract: Video generation enables text-to-video synthesis, video editing, and motion-controlled content creation. However, current video generation models suffer from high computational latency, rendering true real-time capabilities infeasible for downstream tasks. We address this limitation by exploiting the temporal redundancy inherent in video latent patches. To this end, we propose the $\textbf{Latent Inter-frame Pruning with Attention Recovery (LIPAR)}$ framework, which detects and skips recomputing duplicated latent patches. Additionally, we introduce a novel $\textbf{Attention Recovery}$ mechanism that approximates the attention values of pruned tokens, thereby removing visual artifacts arising from naively applying the pruning method. Empirically, our method increases generation throughput by $1.45\times$, on average achieving 12.2 FPS on an NVIDIA A6000 compared to the baseline 8.4 FPS. The proposed method does not compromise generation quality and can be seamlessly integrated with Diffusion Transformer without additional training. Our approach effectively bridges the gap between traditional compression algorithms and modern generative pipelines.
